Unpopular opinion: most productivity advice is written by people who've never had a real deadline.

The whole 'batch your emails' thing? Cool in theory.

But when a client needs something by 3pm and you're batching until 4pm, that's a problem.

Here's what I've learned after 6 years of remote work:

What actually works is checking email when it makes sense for YOUR work. Not when some guru says you should.

The best system is the one you'll actually use. Not the one that looks good in a LinkedIn post.

I tried every productivity system out there. Pomodoro. Time blocking. Inbox zero. Getting Things Done.

The one that stuck? A simple daily list of three things. That's it.

Complicated systems create more overhead than they save.

What productivity advice do you secretly ignore?

#Productivity #RemoteWork

Confession: I still connect to coffee shop WiFi without a VPN sometimes.

I know. Bad habit.

But the VPN I'm testing keeps dropping connections and reconnecting mid-task is genuinely annoying.

Doesn't change the fact that public WiFi is sketchy though.

Here's what most people don't realize:

Someone with basic tools can watch what you're doing. Packet sniffing takes maybe 5 minutes to learn. I've seen it done at a conference once. Guy was just sitting there casually capturing login credentials.

What I actually want to find:

- A VPN that stays connected
- Doesn't tank my speed
- Doesn't require babysitting

Simple ask. Harder to find than you'd think.

Testing 3 right now. Eliminating candidates weekly.

3 years into remote work and I finally figured out lighting.

Spent way too long looking washed out on video calls. Bought a fancy ring light. Hated it. Made me look like I was being interrogated.

The solution that actually worked?

Moved my desk to face the window.

Free. Natural. Doesn't make me look like a suspect.

Sometimes the answer isn't more gear. It's just rearranging what you already have.

I see people dropping $200 on camera setups when the real problem is they're backlit by a window behind them.

Flip your desk around. See what happens.

The low-tech solution is often the right one.

#RemoteWork #HomeOffice

Physical notebooks in 2024. Hear me out.

Yeah I've got Notion, Apple Notes, whatever else.

But when I'm thinking through something complicated—like mapping out an article or debugging a problem—paper still wins.

Something about the lack of tabs and notifications. My brain works differently when the screen isn't involved.

Not saying ditch your note apps.

Just saying the productivity tool that works best might be the one that's been around for centuries.

Mine's a cheap graph paper notebook from the office supply store. $10. Use it daily.

The most sophisticated tool I own is also the simplest.

Sometimes the low-tech solution IS the solution.

Finally figured out why I was exhausted after video calls.

Wasn't the calls themselves.

It was the back-to-back scheduling. No buffer. One call ends at 2:00. Next starts at 2:00. Zero time to process, make notes, or just breathe.

Now I block 15 minutes after every call. Non-negotiable.

The result?

Productivity actually went up. I'm not trying to context-switch while still thinking about the last conversation. Notes get written while they're fresh. Ideas don't slip away.

Small change. Big difference.

The fix that transformed my energy levels cost me nothing. Just a calendar setting.

If you're ending days exhausted from calls, try adding buffers. See what changes.

#RemoteWork #Productivity

Tested my first password manager for 3 weeks straight.

Intentionally tried to break it.

Logged in from random devices. Forgot my master password on purpose (terrifying). Tried the autofill on sketchy sites. Tested the family sharing feature.

Verdict: surprisingly solid. Few complaints but nothing major.

The real test though?

What happens when you lose access to your main device.

That recovery flow is where most password managers fall apart. This one handled it okay. Not great—just okay.

Full comparison coming in January. Testing 2 more before I make recommendations.

What do you care about most in a password manager? Speed? Security? Cross-device sync?

#Cybersecurity #Productivity

The website blocker I use has paid for itself 10x over.

Not because I lack discipline.

Because the internet is literally designed to steal your attention. Every site has a team of engineers optimizing for engagement. I'm one person with deadlines.

Blocking YouTube and Twitter during work hours isn't weakness. It's leveling the playing field.

Takes me about 3 seconds to unblock if I actually need something. But that tiny friction is enough to break the autopilot habit.

The apps aren't the problem. The infinite scroll is.

I'm not fighting my willpower anymore. I'm just removing the temptation.

Works better than any productivity system I've tried.

Wrapped up my first month of serious VPN testing.

Ran speed tests from coffee shops, airports, hotels. Different countries, different servers, different times of day.

The differences are wild.

Same VPN, different location, completely different experience.

What surprised me most:

The marketing claims don't match reality. 'Fastest VPN' means nothing without context. Fast where? Under what conditions? At what time of day?

I've got a clear favorite now. Writing up the full comparison.

If you're paying for a VPN and frustrated with the speeds, the detailed breakdown drops in January.

Christmas morning and I'm not working.

Radical concept, I know.

Took me years to stop feeling guilty about time off. The freelancer brain never fully shuts down. There's always something you could be doing. An email to send. A task to complete. A client to follow up with.

But burnout is real. And it sneaks up on you.

Learned that the hard way 2 years ago. Worked through every holiday. Started January exhausted. Took months to recover.

Now I protect rest like I protect deadlines. Both are non-negotiable.

Happy holidays to everyone who needs permission to log off today.

This is it. You have permission. Close the laptop.

#WorkLifeBalance #FreelanceLife

Holiday travel means working from weird places.

Last year I did client calls from:

- A hotel lobby in Portugal
- A ferry (yes, really)
- My parents' basement (terrible WiFi)
- A parked car (only quiet spot available)

The gear that actually mattered:

Noise canceling headphones saved me on the ferry. Portable charger because outlets are never where you need them. VPN because hotel WiFi is sketchy.

Laptop stand honestly didn't matter when moving around constantly. Ergonomics go out the window when you're improvising.

The lesson: pack light, pack smart, expect chaos.

What's your essential travel work setup?

#DigitalNomad #RemoteWork

Learned something about contracts this year that changed everything:

The payment terms matter more than the rate.

Getting paid $100/hour NET-60 sounds great. Until you realize you're floating 2 months of work on your own dime. Cash flow dies. Stress builds.

Meanwhile $80/hour NET-15 means you're actually getting paid while the project is still fresh in your mind.

Started being way pickier about payment terms this year. Lost a few potential clients.

Zero regrets.

Cash flow beats hourly rate every time. The math doesn't lie.

If you're freelancing and accepting NET-60 terms, you might want to reconsider. That 'higher rate' is costing you more than you think.

Did a full expense tracking audit this week.

Looking at what I spent on tools and subscriptions over the year.

The findings were... embarrassing.

- Paying for 3 things that do basically the same job
- That 'free trial' I forgot to cancel? Still charging me
- The annual subscription math usually works out (switched a few monthlies)

But here's the bigger discovery:

I've been underreporting home office expenses for taxes.

That standing desk, monitors, even part of the internet bill—all potentially deductible if you're self-employed.

Gonna be more careful about tracking next year. Probably saving a few hundred in taxes I was leaving on the table.

Hot take: Slack is not the problem.

How we use Slack is the problem.

I've seen teams where Slack is a nightmare of notifications and urgency. Constant pings. Immediate response expected. Anxiety machine.

And teams where it's calm and async. Status updates respected. Responses on your own schedule.

Same tool. Different culture.

The tool doesn't create the chaos. The expectation that everyone should respond immediately creates the chaos.

Set your status. Mute channels. Check on your schedule.

Slack is supposed to work for you. Not the other way around.

If your Slack feels chaotic, the problem might not be Slack.

#RemoteWork #Productivity

Christmas week productivity tip:

Don't fight it.

Most clients slow down. Meetings get canceled. Emails go unanswered until January.

Use it.

Wrap up loose ends. Do that admin work you've been avoiding. Plan next quarter. Update your systems.

Or honestly? Just take some time off.

The hustle culture take of 'grind while everyone else is resting' sounds good but burns you out. I tried it a few years back. Started January exhausted.

This year I'm doing the opposite. Light work through the holidays. Full reset before 2026.

Your January self will thank you.

What's your holiday work plan?

The backup strategy that saved me twice this year: the 3-2-1 rule.

3 copies of everything.
2 different storage types (like laptop + cloud).
1 offsite (cloud counts).

Here's how it paid off:

September: Lost my laptop charger for a week. Had everything on cloud. Kept working from my phone and a borrowed laptop.

November: Cloud storage had an outage. Had local copies of everything important.

Neither situation became a crisis because the backup was already there.

Paranoid? Maybe. But also never lost a day of work.

The 20 minutes it takes to set this up is nothing compared to the disaster of losing everything.

Year end reflection: what I got wrong about remote work tools this year.

Thought I needed more monitors. Turns out one good one is enough. The second just became a Slack screen.

Thought expensive keyboard was worth it. Honestly my $50 one works fine. The $200 mechanical keyboard lives in a drawer now.

Thought I needed every productivity app. Actually just use 3 regularly. The rest were digital clutter.

The pattern: simpler worked better.

Less switching between tools. Less decision fatigue. More actual work.

2026 approach: minimal. One tool per job. Master it instead of constantly trying new stuff.

Anyone else getting tool fatigue?

#Productivity #RemoteWork

Planning for 2026 and doing something different this year.

No massive goal list. No '10X my revenue' nonsense.

Just 3 things I want to be better at by December. That's it. Three.

Why?

More realistic. Actually achievable. Leaves room for the stuff you can't predict.

Last year I had 47 goals on my list. Completed maybe 8. Felt like a failure even though I actually had a good year.

This year:

1. Finish the VPN comparison series
2. Build the email list to 1,000
3. Take an actual vacation

Simple. Specific. Done.

What's your approach to goal setting?

#Productivity #NewYear

2024 tool verdict: what I'm keeping vs dropping.

Keeping:

- 1Password (tried others, this one just works everywhere)
- Notion (yeah I know everyone uses it—it's actually good though)
- Current VPN (naming it in the full review dropping January)

Dropping:

- That second project management tool I never opened
- Cloud storage service #2 (consolidating everything)
- Premium Zoom (Google Meet is free and fine for my needs)

The subscriptions add up fast. Did the math: I was spending $300/month on tools. Cut it to maybe $150.

That's $1,800/year back in my pocket.

What are you keeping or dropping for next year?
